name: WE0913A (2022 rocket body)
short_status: Hit the far side on Mar 4, 2022 and left a double crater, 18 m and 16 m wide, imaged by LRO at 5.226 N, 234.486 E. First identified as a SpaceX stage, later reattributed to a Chinese booster; officially it remains unattributed.
tagline: Unattributed, evidence points to China · Rocket debris · 2022 · The robotic return Debris impact
stats: overlapping craters, 18 m and 16 m across

facts.label: Impact
facts.value: 4 Mar 2022, on the lunar far side in the Hertzsprung region. Nothing was in position to observe it.

facts.label: The crater
facts.value: A double crater at 5.226 N, 234.486 E: an eastern crater 18 m across superimposed on a western crater 16 m across, about 28 m at its longest. Imaged by LRO's narrow-angle camera on 21 May 2022 and published 23 Jun 2022. LROC notes no other rocket body impact has left a double crater; the four Apollo S-IVB craters were all single and over 35 m.

facts.label: Why two craters
facts.value: The double shape surprised researchers. A spent stage normally has its mass concentrated at the engine end, which would make one crater; two suggest large masses at both ends of the body.

facts.label: The misidentification
facts.value: Bill Gray identified the object in 2015 as the Falcon 9 stage from the DSCOVR launch. In February 2022 Jon Giorgini of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory pointed out that DSCOVR's trajectory never took it near the Moon. Gray publicly corrected himself and reidentified it as a Chang'e 5-T1 booster.

facts.label: The reattribution
facts.value: A peer-reviewed study in The Planetary Science Journal (Campbell et al., Nov 2023) analysed the object's brightness and spin and concluded it was the Long March 3C upper stage from Chang'e 5-T1.

facts.label: Official position
facts.value: NASA and the LRO camera team never attributed the impactor to any country or company: their image was titled "Mystery Rocket Body Found!" and they wrote that the identity remains unclear. Chinese officials denied the booster was theirs.

facts.label: Why it matters now
facts.value: The same researchers frame the 2026 Falcon 9 impact as the calibration case this one could not be: because 2025-010D's origin is independently known, it becomes a benchmark for identifying future cislunar objects of uncertain origin.

timeline: Chang'e 5-T1 launches from Xichang on a Long March 3C. Its upper stage is left in a high orbit.
Bill Gray identifies a drifting object as the Falcon 9 upper stage from the DSCOVR launch. The identification stands unchallenged for seven years.
Gray calculates that the object, catalogued WE0913A, will hit the Moon. The story goes worldwide as a SpaceX rocket about to strike the Moon.
Jon Giorgini of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory emails Gray to point out that DSCOVR's trajectory never took it near the Moon. Gray rechecks and publicly corrects himself.
Impact on the far side, in the Hertzsprung region. Nothing was in position to observe it.
LRO's narrow-angle camera photographs the site and finds not one crater but two, overlapping.
LROC publishes the image under the title "Mystery Rocket Body Found!", stating the identity of the impactor remains unclear.
A peer-reviewed study in The Planetary Science Journal analyses the object's brightness and spin and concludes it was the Long March 3C stage.
